items.title: Who will be the next James Bond?
items.text: Reports indicate that final auditions are currently underway to select the next James Bond. Actors Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor, and Callum Turner emerge as top contenders . Screen tests are reportedly evaluating finalists across three critical criteria: stunt capabilities, dialogue performance, and overall screen presence. Industry analysts highlight Jack Lowden as the current betting favorite and note his potential for a dramatic character transformation. Meanwhile, Josh O’Connor brings acclaimed dramatic experience, and Callum Turner offers a classic, retro aesthetic. Experts also suggest that studio executives might still surprise audiences by choosing an unexpected actor, such as Jacob Elordi. The rigorous selection process aims to ensure the new 007 appeals to a global audience under Amazon MGM Studios, with an official announcement expected around Christmas. Difficult words: contender (a person who competes for a position, prize, or title), stunt (an action that requires physical skill and strength, performed to entertain people in a film or show), acclaimed (publicly praised or celebrated), rigorous (extremely thorough, careful, and demanding strict adherence to standards). items.title: Who will be the next James Bond?
items.text: Actors Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor, and Callum Turner are reportedly in the final auditions to play the next James Bond. Jack Lowden is currently the favorite among betting groups, though all three actors bring special styles to the famous role. Studio executives hope to make a press announcement around Christmas to reveal the new 007 actor to fans worldwide. Difficult words: audition (a short performance by an actor, singer, or dancer to show their ability for a role), stunt (a dangerous or difficult action done in a movie), screen presence (when an actor can get the audience’s attention whenever they appear on camera). items.title: The longest train
items.text: South Africa’s state-owned logistics company, Transnet, has successfully tested a 7.6-kilometre freight train and claimed to set a new world record. In a test journey, the colossal train, powered by a combination of electric and diesel locomotives, consisted of 696 empty wagons and covered 860 kilometers between a western coastal port and an inland iron ore mine. According to company officials, the test run surpassed the previous record established in 2001 by a 7.2-kilometre freight train operating in Western Australia. Transnet presented the successful trial as a significant breakthrough for the nation’s freight transport network, which relies heavily on efficient rail systems to export raw minerals. However, industry observers note that the record claim currently originates directly from Transnet itself, and they await external verification . Difficult words: colossal (extremely large), iron ore (a natural rock or mineral from which metallic iron can be extracted), verification (establishing the truth, accuracy, or validity of something). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: The longest train
items.text: A state-owned logistics company in South Africa successfully tested a freight train which is 7.6 kilometres long. The train consists of 696 empty wagons and recently travelled 860 kilometres from a port on the west coast to a mine . Electric and diesel engines placed along the train provided all the power needed to move it. The company says this train is officially longer than the previous record-holder, an Australian train tested back in 2001. The company called the successful test a milestone for the country’s train network, which helps move materials across long distances. Although only the company announced the new world record, many people are excited about this big step forward for African railway transportation. Difficult words: logistics (transporting goods to customers), freight (goods transported by truck, train, ship, or plane), mine (a deep hole in the earth from which workers get coal, minerals, or stones), milestone (an important event in the history of something). items.title: The longest train

items.title: Study finds majority of pilots nod off mid-flight
items.text: A new report has raised serious concerns about pilot fatigue. The European Cockpit Association (ECA) conducted a survey of nearly 7,200 pilots across 32 countries. It discovered that exhaustion in the cockpit is a widespread and underreported problem. More than three-quarters of respondents said they had briefly dozed off while operating an aircraft in the month before the survey. Almost a quarter of them admitted they continued flying even when they were too tired. Furthermore, half said they had operated a flight when they should have declared themselves unfit for duty. Tiredness can result from long working hours, insufficient rest, and unpredictable schedules. The pilots were very frank in their answers to the survey questions. Many said they were reluctant to report fatigue because they feared punishment or other negative reactions from their bosses. Captain Coen George, a director of the ECA, warned: "When pilots fear career consequences, fatigue goes unreported and the risk returns to the cockpit." Aviation safety experts say exhaustion can impair judgement, slow reaction times and prevent pilots from responding effectively to unexpected in-flight situations. The experts urged airlines to foster a culture in which pilots can report tiredness without fear of repercussions. Carriers should ensure that passenger safety is their top priority. items.title: World-famous London shopping street pedestrianized
items.text: One of London's most famous shopping streets has been pedestrianized. This means no cars, buses, trucks, or motorbikes can enter it. The street is called Oxford Street. It is well known all over the world. It used to be full of traffic. The Mayor of London, Sir Sadiq Khan, decided to make it pedestrian-only. Around one kilometre of the street is off limits to vehicles. However, delivery trucks can use the area between midnight and 7 am. Mayor Khan hopes the pedestrianization will bring more shoppers back to the area. He called it a very important event for London. Mr Khan also plans to plant more trees along the street, create public squares, and add more seats and tables. There have been mixed reactions to the pedestrianization of Oxford Street. Many people support the plan. They are happy that the area will be less polluted. Khan said a traffic-free Oxford Street would "unlock the full potential" of an important area of London and help make a better, greener, and richer London. Around half a million people visit the street every day. However, many Londoners are unhappy that the street has been closed to traffic. Local official Tim Barnes said: "Traffic will be pushed to the small streets nearby causing economic and environmental harm." The Spectator magazine warned that life for car drivers would be harder. items.title: Mummy removed from exhibition over 'lack of consent'
items.text: A museum in Scotland has removed the remains of an ancient Egyptian mummy from an exhibition because there is no documented evidence that the deceased gave consent for their remains to be displayed. Glasgow's Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum took away the remains of a priest named Nakht, a mummified male head, and other body parts. In place of the exhibits, visitors found signs explaining that the remains had been removed "as a mark of respect". The museum said the decision "reflects contemporary museum practice". It added: "In the absence of consent, we believe removing ancient Egyptian human remains from display is more respectful to the deceased individuals." The decision has provoked widespread criticism. Scottish politician Murdo Fraser called the move "woke madness". He argued that museums should showcase history rather than hide it. A museum visitor complained that his daughter was upset at not being able to see the exhibits. An education campaigner said the decision "represents the triumph of educational stupidity and ignorance". He added: "It is not possible to seek permission from those who died thousands of years ago." However, the museum defended its action. It cited the International Council of Museums' Code of Ethics, which says museums "should uphold the inherent dignity of human remains". Buy my 1,000 Ideas and Activities for Language Teachers eBook. items.title: Man sells everything for AI dream "partner"
items.text: A man in Brazil had a sad experience in his search for love. Mr X, 49, sold everything he owned to get enough money to see a woman he met online. He travelled over 2,000 kilometres by bus. He first met her online in 2020 and fell in love with her. He wanted to marry her. Her name was Jessica. Her online profile read: "I really want to support you. I want you to come to my farm and never work again in your life." Mr X went to meet her in the city of Belo Horizonte, but he could not find her. He showed people photos of her, but nobody knew who she was. He then found out that she was not real. She was created by AI. The man was sad. He said: "I came here to find happiness." Mr X's story shows how risky it can be to look for love online. Many people feel lonely and want to find a partner. However, they can be easily tricked because AI can make people who look and sound real. Jessica's social media account had over 300,000 followers. She looked like a real woman. The person who created Jessica said they made her to get people's attention online. They wanted to use the AI Jessica to help sell things. Mr X wants people to be careful so they don't make a similar mistake in the future. It is important to check the identity of a person you meet online carefully. The man said: "Sometimes, loneliness at home causes many problems in a person's life." Buy my 1,000 Ideas and Activities for Language Teachers eBook. items.title: Why you forget English words and how to fix it
items.text: Many students try to memorize English words and feel frustrated when they forget them. They repeat vocabulary again and again, but the effect is temporary . The issue isn’t memory. It is the learning strategy. Words without context are difficult to keep. The brain needs connections to store information effectively. Stories create those connections. They give words meaning and show how they work in real situations. When you listen to a story and imagine it, you engage your brain fully. You connect the words to real pictures in your head. LangoPlay applies this method in a simple way. It offers short, interactive stories where you listen, think, and respond. Each step increases your understanding and helps you remember. Over time, the difference is clear. You keep vocabulary longer and use it more confidently. If you want to stop forgetting words, stop relying on memorization. items.title: Good news of October
items.text: A roundup of positive global developments highlights encouraging progress across conservation, medicine, and technology. Environmental reports reveal that deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon dropped significantly, and lead to the lowest fire activity in decades, while wild tigers returned to Kazakhstan after 70 years. In Canada, Indigenous nations partnered with the federal government to establish a massive marine reserve. Medical breakthroughs feature a world-first eye implant that restores vision for patients with age-related macular degeneration , a fast 10-second liquid treatment stopping tooth decay in children, and a new mRNA flu vaccine showing improved effectiveness. Meanwhile, global public health initiatives reached historic milestones. HIV infections have fallen to a 30-year low, and digital tracking helps health workers vaccinate over 200,000 previously unreached children in Nigeria. Finally, European regulations now require digital watermarks on AI, and global electric vehicle sales surged to nearly 30 percent of total market share. Difficult words: implant (a medical device, tissue, or object that is placed inside the body through surgery), macular degeneration (an eye disease that causes vision loss in the center of the field of vision as people age), watermark (a hidden or visible digital mark in a file or image to identify its source). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Good news of October
items.text: This month brings positive news from around the world in nature, health, and clean technology. Amazon deforestation dropped by nearly 40 percent, and reduced forest fires, while wild tigers were returned to Kazakhstan. In Canada, Indigenous communities teamed up with the government to protect a huge ocean area. In health news, a tiny eye implant approved in Europe helps bring back lost vision , and a fast liquid treatment stops tooth decay in young children without drilling. Also, global HIV infections dropped to their lowest level in 30 years, and new digital tracking helped health teams vaccinate 200,000 children in Nigeria. Lastly, European laws now want clear labels on AI videos, and electric cars made up almost 30 percent of new global car sales. Difficult words: deforestation (cutting down forests and trees across a wide area), implant (a tiny piece of medical equipment placed inside the body to help it work), vision (the ability to see things with your eyes), decay (damage to your tooth). items.title: One billion meals thrown away every day
items.text: More than one billion meals are thrown away worldwide every day, despite famine and millions of people starving. The United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) recently reported that households are responsible for 60 per cent of food waste, followed by restaurants and food services at 28 per cent, and shops at 12 per cent. The Maldives has the highest estimated household food waste per person, at around 260 kilograms annually. Syria, Seychelles, Mexico and Tunisia also recorded high levels. Globally, food waste accounts for 8 to 10 per cent of greenhouse gas emissions. As discarded food decomposes in landfills, it releases the dangerous greenhouse gas methane, which accelerates global warming. Individuals, businesses and governments can all take practical steps to reduce food waste. People should plan meals, prepare shopping lists, and purchase only what they need. We should store ingredients correctly and freeze surplus portions. We should also turn leftovers into new dishes and compost inedible waste. Restaurants and supermarkets also have a huge part to play in reducing food loss. They can donate surplus food to communities in need. Martin Krause, Director of the Climate Change Division at UNEP, said: "Every meal rescued, shared or never wasted is food put to better use." items.title: Made in Qatar
items.text: Qatar is actively expanding its national production to diversify its economy and build a strong global reputation for homegrown brands. Local agricultural and food companies are leading this movement by boosting food security through fully integrated, sustainable farming systems. For example, major local producers have increased fresh poultry supply to meet almost all domestic demand while developing zero-waste operations powered by solar energy and recycled water. At the same time, health-conscious entrepreneurs are introducing plant-based foods and cold-pressed juices to fill gaps in the market. Beyond agriculture, strategic investment firms are supporting unique industrial ventures , including the country’s first electric vehicle factory. Together, these initiatives show how Qatar is moving beyond its traditional energy sector. The country empowers local talent and creates high-quality, sustainable products capable of competing on the international stage. Difficult words: reputation (the opinion that people generally have about how good, reliable, or successful someone or something is), entrepreneur (a person who starts and runs their own business), venture (a new business activity or project).
